summary: Western passports — the US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas — enter Guatemala visa-free for up to 90 days, a stay shared across the CA-4 zone with El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. Other nationalities need a consular visa, and some also require a security-vetted "consulted" visa.

conditionalWaivers.text: Travelers holding a valid US visa (category B1/B2 or higher), or a valid Canadian or Schengen visa or residence permit, are normally admitted to Guatemala without a Guatemalan visa for up to 90 days in the CA-4 area. The exemption does not cover nationalities on Guatemala's restricted list, which always need prior consular approval.

fee.notes: Around USD 25–50 depending on the consulate and entry type; issued for stays of up to 90 days.
Fee varies by consulate. Applications are referred to the Guatemalan Institute of Migration for security vetting before the consulate may issue the visa. Allow several weeks.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months on arrival in Guatemala.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required only for travelers arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission (parts of South America and Africa). Not needed on direct arrivals from North America or Europe.

travelInsurance.text: Not an entry requirement, but recommended — private hospitals in Guatemala City require payment or proof of insurance up front.

onwardTicket.text: Airlines routinely require a return or onward ticket before boarding, and immigration officers may ask for one on arrival.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; officers may ask visitors to show means of support for their stay.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of USD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure.

notes: Pre-Columbian artefacts are national heritage — buying, possessing or exporting them is a crime.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in Guatemala City, Antigua and larger hotels, but the country runs on cash. Carry quetzales in small notes for markets, shuttles and everything around Lake Atitlán and Tikal. US dollars are easy to exchange but rarely accepted directly outside tourist hubs.

safety.text: Violent crime and armed robbery are real concerns, though the main tourist circuit — Antigua, Lake Atitlán, Tikal — is well policed and mostly sees petty theft. Use registered shuttles or app taxis rather than public buses, keep valuables out of sight, and avoid remote roads after dark.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Guatemala travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: The dry season from November to April is ideal for volcano hikes, Antigua and Tikal; the rainy season (May to October) usually still has clear mornings, with downpours in the afternoon.

idp.text: Guatemala is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Guatemala is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Guatemala yet.

tips.text: Guatemala shares one 90-day stay with El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua (the CA-4). Hopping between the four does not reset your clock — extend at the migration institute or leave the zone (Mexico and Belize both count) before day 90.
A one-time extension of up to 90 further days is available from the Instituto Guatemalteco de Migración in Guatemala City. Start the paperwork well before your first 90 days run out.
PROATUR, Guatemala's tourist assistance service, runs a 24/7 hotline on 1500 (English spoken) and can advise on routes or arrange security escorts for less-visited areas.
The Acatenango overnight hike reaches almost 4,000 m — cold, high and strenuous. Go with an established operator, and watch Fuego's eruptions from the designated viewpoints only.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Guatemala?
faq.answer: Most Western travelers do not: the US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and most of the Americas enter visa-free for up to 90 days. Other nationalities need a consular visa (Category B), and some require a security-vetted consulted visa (Category C). Check your category with a Guatemalan consulate.

faq.question: How does the CA-4 90-day rule work in Guatemala?
faq.answer: Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua share one migration zone: your 90 days cover all four countries combined, and crossing between them does not reset the count. To stay longer, apply for a one-time extension at the migration institute or leave the zone — Mexico and Belize are both outside it.

faq.question: Can I do a border run to reset my 90 days?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Leaving to Mexico or Belize and returning does not automatically grant a fresh 90 days. Officers can re-admit you for the balance of your original stay. The clean options are the official extension or a genuine break outside the CA-4.

faq.question: Is Guatemala safe for tourists?
faq.answer: The main tourist circuit — Antigua, Lake Atitlán, Quetzaltenango, Tikal — sees large numbers of visitors with mostly petty-crime incidents, but Guatemala does have high overall crime levels. Stick to registered shuttles, avoid night driving, keep valuables hidden, and use the 1500 PROATUR hotline if you need help.

faq.question: What money should I use in Guatemala?
faq.answer: The quetzal (GTQ). Cards work in cities and better hotels, but much of the country is cash-only. Carry small notes, and withdraw from ATMs attached to banks. US dollars are simple to exchange but rarely accepted as payment outside airports and big hotels.
